first_impression.reaction: We Googled this half out of curiosity because Bali is on the shortlist. The intro is refreshingly un-salesy: 'There is no single Indonesian wedding.' tells me this isn't going to be a listicle of tacky 'exotic touches'. The line 'If you are drawn to Bali, or marrying into an Indonesian family, the last part covers what makes a wedding there legal' is what actually kept us going, because the legal side is the bit we worry about. I skimmed the culture sections and read the legal part properly.

journey.quote: Some details are recorded by a royal palace, a university journal or UNESCO. Others are simply often told, and we say so.
journey.reaction: Honest about what's sourced and what's folklore. That's the opposite of the usual wedding blog fluff. Trust goes up.

journey.quote: Siraman falls before the core rites, so elders who pour the water need to arrive a day or two early, and their flights and rooms should be planned around it.
journey.reaction: This is exactly the kind of thing we think about: our grandparents and flights. A practical planning note inside a culture section reads like someone who has actually run one of these weekends.

journey.section: The Javanese wedding, step by step
journey.quote: In the palace account they take turns throwing rolled betel leaves (gantal) at each other, the groom first; then the bride washes the groom's feet and an egg is broken.
journey.reaction: Interesting, but neither of us is Javanese, so this is the part where I start skimming. The repeated 'in the palace account' and 'it is often told' gets a bit academic for a skim read.

journey.quote: None of this is a show for guests. If a Balinese family invites you, follow the priest and the family, dress as they ask and keep cameras down unless told otherwise.
journey.reaction: Good. Our biggest social fear is looking try-hard or culturally tone-deaf in front of friends. This tells me the brand won't sell us a 'Balinese blessing experience' as a costume.

journey.section: Which Balinese dances suit a reception
journey.quote: For a reception, ask the troupe which dances are performed for audiences, and leave sacred dances to the temple.
journey.reaction: Useful and specific. This is the one custom we might actually include, and now I know the right question to ask.

journey.section: Can Australians marry legally in Bali?
journey.quote: Registries do not normally accept a CNI issued more than three months earlier, so time it carefully.
journey.reaction: This is the insider detail I wanted. Concrete timing, sourced to the Embassy. As a lawyer I appreciate that it's framed as general information, not advice.

journey.section: Can Australians marry legally in Bali?
journey.quote: both partners must hold the same religion, and if not, one must convert.
journey.reaction: This is a big deal for us and I didn't know it. It's an honest trade-off stated plainly. It makes me think we'd probably do the legal bit in Sydney and a celebration in Bali, but the page doesn't actually spell out that option, which is what I'm now wondering.

journey.section: Can Australians marry legally in Bali?
journey.quote: On the Embassy's guidance, a ceremony that is not registered is not a legal marriage, so treat a blessing on its own as a celebration only.
journey.reaction: Clear and honest. It hints at the 'marry at home, celebrate in Bali' route without quite saying it. I'd like one sentence that says whether that is a common, sensible path.

journey.section: Can Australians marry legally in Bali?
journey.quote: Indonesia's revised criminal code includes penalties for cohabitation and sex outside marriage, and Aceh applies Sharia law.
journey.reaction: Appreciate the honesty, though it leaves me with a slightly uneasy question about what this means for unmarried guests sharing rooms in Bali. It's raised and then left hanging.

journey.section: Can Australians marry legally in Bali?
journey.quote: a Wedded Advisor can be your single point of contact for the rest of the plan, with the fee and inclusions agreed in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: 'Fee and inclusions agreed in writing' speaks straight to our hidden-costs fear and our 'what does end-to-end actually mean' question. Single point of contact is what we want. Not pushy.

journey.quote: Whether you are honouring a partner's family or simply drawn to Bali, the best wedding there starts with the right questions.
journey.reaction: Soft, fine. Slightly generic as a closer, but no cliché and no hard sell.

unanswered_questions: If we're not the same religion, is the usual route to marry legally in Australia first and have a celebration or blessing in Bali? Does Wedded Wonderland arrange that?
What does the cohabitation law mean in practice for unmarried couples among our guests sharing rooms in Bali?
Has Wedded Wonderland actually run weddings in Bali? Is there a real wedding with venue and date we can look at?
Who is physically on the ground in Bali on the day: your own people or local suppliers you hand us to?
How long does the CNI and registry process take end to end, and would the advisor coordinate the timing with us?
would_share_with: Partner (the legal section, as a 'did you know about the religion rule?')
Parents (the respectful-customs section, since they're paying a share and will want guests briefed)

cta_reaction.quote: When you are ready, speak with a Wedded Advisor
cta_reaction.why: The tone is right and the 'fee and inclusions agreed in writing' line helps a lot. But this is our first post, we haven't picked a destination and I haven't seen a real Bali wedding from them yet. I'd bookmark it, read the Bali destination page and look for a real wedding before enquiring.

top_3_changes: In the legal section, add one plain sentence on the route many Australian couples take when they don't share a religion (for example, legal ceremony at home, celebration in Bali), if it can be sourced.
Link a real Bali wedding (venue and date) near the secondary CTA so couples like us have proof before we enquire.
Either explain briefly what the cohabitation provision means for a wedding group in Bali, with a source, or point to where to check; right now it raises a worry and leaves it.
